newsitem.title: CHINA: China debt depository seen aiding debt trade.
newsitem.headline: China debt depository seen aiding debt trade.

text.p: China's newly launched central state debt depository will help unify and regulate state debt trading once it is fully operational by the end of this year, financial analysts said on Tuesday.
"The full operation of the depository will bring an end to the scattered nature of China's state debt trading," said an investment analyst.
"Irregularities will be effectively checked, making the state debt market much more regulated," he said.
The China Government Securities Depository Trust and Clearing Co, based in Beijing, was already clearing debt trading by the nation's state-run banks, they said.
Non-banking financial institutions were expected to move their positions to the depository for clearing before the end of the year, they said.
The depository, set up in February to coordinate domestic debt trading, provides trust services, clearing and settling of all state debt transactions.

In early June, Beijing ordered state banks to cease state debt trading on the nation's stock exchanges and local trading centres and to confine their debt trading to China's interbank market based in Shanghai.
Since then, industry sources said, the banks had moved all their state debt positions to the depository.
Beijing has ordered all local exchanges and state debt trading centres to shift their positions to the depository.
It has also told all securities brokerages and trust firms to stop providing trust certificates for holding state debt positions on behalf of customers, the sources said.
Analysts said they expected brokerages and trust firms to shift their positions to the depository by the end of the year, making the unified system fully operational.

The depository was designed to unify China's state debt trading under one clearing system although positions can be traded on all floors of regional exchanges and trading centres, and through off-floor trading, analysts said.
Previously, spot debt purchased in the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges and in regional centres such as Wuhan could only be traded on the exchange where they were purchased.
A lack of effective central supervision had been behind widespread irregularities including short-selling and overdraft trading, which are banned in China, analysts said.
In some cases, the same debt had been used as a deposit to trade repurchase contracts on different exchanges or trading centres, they said.

The depository has so far enrolled over 30 members including more than 20 state banks, the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges, a number of large-sized trust firms and stock brokerages, the China Securities newspapers said on Monday.
It aimed to have more than 500 members by 2000, with some members acting as market-makers, dealers and clearing banks, it said.
The depository expected China to open its state debt market to foreign investors once its currency -- the yuan -- became fully convertible, it said.

China's central bank officials have said the yuan probably would not be made convertible on the capital account until the early years of the next century. It made the yuan convertible on the current account last year.
